name: Central Grebo
confidence_why: No published work describes word stress in Central Grebo itself: Marchese (1986) and Johnson & Hasselbring (2002), the only sources that cover its dialects (Borobo, Dorobo, Trembo, Nyenebo, Globo), give three or four register tones and say nothing about stress, while the lexically contrastive stress reported for 'Grebo' by Innes (1966) and Luckau (1975), and filed under Central Grebo by StressTyp2, describes Glebo and Jabo, i.e. Southern Grebo, a separate language.

world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.quote: Grebo has a system of four tone levels; tone is not marked in Grebo writing, but in this book, where it is necessary to mark tone, this will be shown by numerals. The method of tone marking is: 1. High tone is marked with 1: kg 1 chief 2. High-mid tone is marked with 2: bi 2 beat 3. Low-mid tone is marked with 3: ya 3 bring 4. Low tone is marked with 4: pu 4 swell. Gliding tones are marked with a combination of two (or, rarely, three) numerals joined by a hyphen: hu 3-2 throw

new_statements.rule_in_words: Grebo (Glebo/Seaside dialect) is a four-level register tone language with lexical and grammatical tone (contour tones, verb tone classes, 1st vs 2nd person pronouns distinguished by tone). Neither this nor any other opened source mentions word stress, stress placement, or the absence of stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None; stress not discussed at all.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is given on citation forms and in phrases (pronoun tone varies by context). Source describes Glebo = Southern Grebo [grj] sout2826, not Central Grebo [grv]; only pp. 11-15 of the phonological chapters are in the open excerpt, so a stress remark on pp. 16-19 cannot be excluded.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog/Ethnologue split Grebo into five ISO languages; Central Grebo [grv] cent2041 (dialects Nyenebo, Dorobo, Borobo, Trembo) has no grammar, phonology or sketch of its own (Glottolog lists no grammar, sketch or phonology). Every phonological description of 'Grebo' (Innes 1960/1966/1967/1981, Luckau 1975, Sapir 1931 on Jabo/Gweabo, Wilson 1838, Payne 1860/1864, Auer 1870, Müller 1877, Christaller 1890) is of Glebo/Seaside Grebo of Cape Palmas or of Jabo, which Glottolog codes as Southern Grebo [grj] sout2826. The quoted Innes 1966 statement therefore belongs to sout2826, not cent2041.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Innes 1966 statement (tone language) but adds, second-hand, that Innes 1966 and Luckau 1975 treat stress in Grebo as contrastive; the existing reading 'tone language, no stress statement' rests on a five-page Rosetta excerpt of Innes 1966 (pp. 11-15) and, per Marchese, Innes 1966 does make a stress claim somewhere in its remaining pages (not available to us). The claim describes Glebo/Jabo = Southern Grebo [grj] sout2826, so for Central Grebo it is at best an inference across dialects.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Marchese gives no stress rule of her own: Kru languages have three or four register tones (lexical and grammatical), and, second-hand, she reports that Innes 1966 and Luckau 1975 claim that stress in Grebo is contrastive (i.e. lexically distinctive), while noting there is no systematic study of stress in Kru. No placement is stated. Innes 1966 describes Glebo (Seaside Grebo) and Luckau's dissertation is a tonal analysis of Glebo ('Gebo' as printed) and Jabo, both Southern Grebo [grj], so the claim is about Southern Grebo, not Central Grebo, although Marchese's own Grebo tense/aspect data include the Central dialect Borobo (consultant from Wissiken, Barrobo Chiefdom, p. 9-10). Two other 'stress' hits (pp. 113, 261) concern Cameroonian Pidgin and Neo-Melanesian, not Kru.
new_statements.identity_note: No opened work describes Central Grebo [grv] phonology directly. Innes 1966/1967 and Luckau 1975 (the 'Grebo stress is contrastive' sources named by Marchese) describe Glebo (Seaside Grebo) and Jabo = Southern Grebo [grj] sout2826. Johnson & Hasselbring 2002 covers the Central Grebo dialects (Grimes 1996 'Globo Grebo' = Gblobo, Nyenebo, Dorobo, Borobo, Trembo; Barrobo, Dorobo and Trembo in its word lists and texts) but only at the level of dialect survey and orthography. Marchese 1986's Grebo data include the Central dialect Borobo (Wissiken, Barrobo Chiefdom) alongside Nyabo, but her one stress sentence is a report on the Glebo/Jabo literature.

readall_conflicts: One partial disagreement, second-hand: the existing statement (Innes 1966 p. 12, Rosetta excerpt) reads 'tone language, no stress statement', but Marchese 1986 p. 261 reports that Innes 1966 and Luckau 1975 claim 'stress in Grebo is contrastive'. That claim could not be checked at source (the Innes 1966 excerpts held here, pp. 11-15, contain no stress statement; Innes 1967 is lending-only; Luckau 1975 is an unavailable Stanford dissertation), and both cited works describe Glebo/Jabo = Southern Grebo [grj], not Central Grebo. Johnson & Hasselbring 2002, the only opened work that covers Central Grebo dialects, says nothing about stress and gives three orthographic tones for Grebo vs Innes's four tone levels for Glebo; this is a difference in tone inventory/orthography, not a stress conflict.
